narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 59.2% probability that you will fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only somewhat above a coin flip, not a certainty, but it was high enough to trigger rejection under the admissions process.

The strongest factor pushing toward that prediction was your undergraduate GPA of 3.10, which is below the 3.23 average among accepted students. Next, your first-year class-rank decile of 5, below the accepted-student average of 6, also pushed the prediction toward failure. By contrast, your third-year class-rank decile of 7, above the accepted average of 5.79, pushed toward passing, but it was not strong enough to outweigh the first two factors. Your LSAT score was essentially at the accepted average, so it did not materially change this picture.

To move forward, ask for a human review of the decision and provide context for your undergraduate and first-year performance. Discuss with admissions advisors what evidence or additional coursework could demonstrate improved academic readiness. Consider strengthening your record before reapplying, such as raising your GPA through further study, retaking the LSAT if practice scores suggest meaningful improvement, and documenting any personal circumstances that affected your earlier grades.
